Dr Hussam Abu Safia is seen on a video call from prison during an Israeli Supreme Court hearing of an appeal by his lawyers to end his detention in Jerusalem on June 10, 2026 [File: Handout/Physicians for Human Rights Israel via AP Photo]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
An Israeli court has extended the detention of Hussam Abu Safia, the director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, who remains held without charge amid repeated calls for his release.
Abu Safia’s lawyer said that a court in Beersheba decided on Wednesday to extend the physician’s detention for a further six months, according to Abu Safia’s account on X.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Hundreds of doctors demand World Medical Association suspend Israellist 2 of 3Israeli rights group raises concerns about jailed doctor amid Gaza strikeslist 3 of 3‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcareend of list
The court said that Abu Safia “poses a threat to the State of Israel”, his lawyer reported.
“Dr Hussam questioned why his detention order was being renewed once again, expressing that he is being punished for fulfilling his humanitarian mission and professional duty as a doctor at Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza,” the social media post added.
The Israeli army detained Abu Safia in December 2024, along with other staff members and patients, during a raid on the hospital in northern Gaza.
International agencies and rights groups have called for the physician’s release on multiple occasions, highlighting reports that he is being subjected to abuse in detention.

On Tuesday evening, before a speech to Asian leaders, Trump praised Marcos and his parents, saying, “I just don’t wanna date myself, but I knew your parents very well,” adding that Marcos Jr had “good genetics”.

item.description:

(Al Jazeera)By Alia Chughtai and Mohamed HusseinPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
Donors have pledged about $18bn for Gaza through US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. But more than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin, and nearly 1.4 million Palestinians are still living in makeshift shelters.
Even preliminary reconstruction efforts have stalled. The board had asked for $280m to fund the initial building phase, but in September it said most of that money remained unspent.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without actionlist 2 of 3Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under waylist 3 of 3Palestinians find refuge in ancient caves after Israel demolishes homesend of list
In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board warned that the truce between Israel and Hamas could collapse unless immediate steps are taken to carry out the ceasefire deal, according to The Associated Press.
The next day, on Wednesday, Israel began its first major military ground operation in the Gaza Strip since the ceasefire began, attacking refugee camps in the central part of the enclave.
Since the ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,658 Palestinians and injured 6,000, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Israel continues to block the entry of 60,000 mobile homes promised under the ceasefire deal and to severely restrict food and medical aid into the besieged enclave. It has also yet to allow the Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza to enter the Strip.

Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island.
Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.

A senior World Bank official says Lebanon has been slow to use international aid to rebuild areas destroyed during the 2024 war and the renewed fighting since March 2026.
World Bank managing director of operations Anna Bjerde said she had to be “honest” about the pace of reconstruction during a visit to southern Lebanon on Tuesday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Israel builds 90km network of military roads across southern Lebanonlist 2 of 3More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages, UN sayslist 3 of 3UNIFIL patrol comes under fire in southern Lebanonend of list
The international financial institution approved $250m in June 2025 to help Lebanon clear rubble and repair “damaged critical public infrastructure” after the 2024 Israel-Hezbollah war. But a September progress report showed that only $4.2m had been paid out, a fraction of the projected $100m by July 2026.
The World Bank estimated that rebuilding after the 2024 war would cost about $11b.
“Parliament ratification of the said loan experienced considerable delays,” Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s office responded in a statement, adding that the “worsening security situation” as a result of Israel’s continuing occupation of southern Lebanon “delayed the timely launch of project activities”.Anna Bjerde, the World Bank’s managing director of operations, speaks during an interview with The Associated Press in Beirut on November 17, 2026 [Bilal Hussein/AP Photo]
